By [author name]

At Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from the supplier Benchline. At the end, the workshop decided to keep using it, though not yet for every job.

## The workshop decided how the schedule would work

Fenwick chose Benchline after checking that the software could distinguish those two statuses. The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session, while the team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone.

In an email interview, workshop manager Priya Vale named what had to be settled before the schedule was useful: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The trial summary counts jobs, not repair times

The workshop's own summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. What it documents is the team's reported experience, not a measured change in repair speed.

Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## The manager looks back on the choice

Asked about making the same choice again, and about what to change, Vale replied: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

Managers considering a shared schedule can start with the question Fenwick had to answer: what does ready for work mean at their own benches?
EOF
